title: Shooting inquest to begin this month
subtitle: Andrew Moore killed by police officer
article: --- An inquest will be held later this month into last year's police shooting death of a 35-year-old man in a west-side confectionery.
The inquest into the death of Andrew Moore will be held at Saskatoon Court of Queen's Bench May 24-27.
Moore was fatally shot during an altercation with Saskatoon police inside the Twenty-Ninth Street Confectionery on April 30, 2004.

No criminal charges were laid following an investigation by Saskatoon police and a review of the file by Crown prosecutors, said Lorna Nystuen, director of the coroner's branch of the provincial Justice Department.
A jury will be selected and coroner Doug Kovach will hear evidence from witnesses as he seeks to determine the circumstances of the death.
In the days after the shooting, police Chief Russell Sabo said the officer involved had no choice but to fire a single bullet when Moore, trapped inside the store, pulled out a handgun.
Police did not release the name of the officer, a constable who had 10 years experience at the time.

According to police at the time, the constable was on patrol around 6 p.m. when he saw Moore at the corner of 29th Street and Avenue I, recognizing Moore from previous dealings with him. The officer intended to arrest Moore on warrants. He requested back-up and then advised Moore he was under arrest. Moore ignored him and walked away, Sabo said at the time.

The officer pepper-sprayed Moore to stop him but it had no effect, apparently because Moore was wearing tight, wraparound sunglasses protecting his eyes. The officer went after him again and a chase on foot began.

Sabo said Moore dashed into the confectionery and through it, attempting to get out the back door. The back-up officer was there waiting, but Moore couldn't get the door open. The pursuing constable caught up and tried to apprehend Moore inside the rear of the building. That resulted in a fight between the two, during which the officer saw the gun in Moore's hand, Sabo has said.
In that situation, the weapon is considered to be drawn, he said.
The officer repeatedly ordered Moore to drop the firearm and continued to resist arrest, Sabo said at the time.

A struggle ensued, and the officer felt his life and possibly the lives of others in the vicinity were in peril, according to Sabo. The officer fired a single shot, which hit Moore in the head, he said.
The officer called for an ambulance, but Moore was pronounced dead at the scene.
